extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents/applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining when a document or disclosure (including electronic and nontraditional media) qualifies as a 'printed publication' / prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102, how to establish the date of public accessibility, and related evidentiary rules for examination and reexamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication is a unitary concept
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'printed publication' should be approached as a unitary concept; interpret 'printed' and 'publication' in light of modern technology (e.g., probability of dissemination and public accessibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court decisions (e.g., In re Wyer) indicate the traditional dichotomy between 'printed' and 'publication' is outdated; focus on whether the item was disseminated or made publicly accessible such that interested persons could locate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for printed-publication status
rubrics_metrics.description: The party challenging patentability (petitioner/examiner) bears the burden of establishing that a particular document is a 'printed publication.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If petitioner/examiner fails to carry the burden of proving public accessibility (e.g., Blue Calypso), the reference cannot be relied on as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public accessibility is the touchstone
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference is a 'printed publication' only if it was sufficiently accessible to the public interested in the art; 'public accessibility' is the primary legal test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a case-by-case inquiry considering the facts and circumstances surrounding disclosure; apply the standard that persons interested and ordinarily skilled in the art, exercising reasonable diligence, can locate the reference (quoting Kyocera/Suffolk Tech/Blue Calypso).

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic publications qualify if accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic publications (online databases, internet publications, discussion groups, forums, digital videos, social media posts) are 'printed publications' if accessible to persons concerned with the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce sufficient proof of dissemination or availability; internet pages, database printouts, and newsgroup postings have been treated as prior art when publicly accessible (In re Wyer; Suffolk Tech v. AOL; In re Epstein). Office should retain copies for internet sources that may not be retrievable later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of availability for internet publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet/online publications are publicly available as of the date the item was publicly posted; absent evidence of posting date, the publication cannot be relied on as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no publication/retrieval date is present, examiners may ask the Scientific and Technical Information Center (STIC) to find earliest date of publication or posting (see MPEP § 901.06(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of teachings to be relied upon
rubrics_metrics.description: An electronic publication may be relied upon for all that it would have reasonably suggested to one having ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If relying on an abstract of a patent/printed publication, only the text of the abstract (not the underlying document) may support a 102/103 rejection. When electronic and paper versions differ, cite and rely upon each version as independent references based on their disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wayback Machine captures presumed publicly accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications obtained via the Wayback Machine are prima facie deemed publicly accessible at the date/time in the capture's timestamp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The burden shifts to the applicant to challenge accessibility, authenticity, or reliability of a Wayback Machine capture (see Valve Corp. v. Ironburg Inventions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media may be prior art if publicly accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media posts (YouTube, Twitter, Facebook, public forum posts) can be prior art provided the public accessibility requirements are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate on a case-by-case basis considering where posted, privacy restrictions, length of time posted, whether indexed/searchable, and archival status; timestamps on social media may require careful scrutiny as their reliability can vary; applicants may challenge dates by affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132.

rubrics_metrics.name: No need to prove actual public viewership
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unnecessary to prove that someone actually looked at the document when the publication is accessible to the public through a library or patent office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If accessibility is shown (i.e., disseminated or made available so skilled persons exercising reasonable diligence can locate it), there is no requirement to show specific members of the public received or examined the material (In re Wyer; Jazz Pharm.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis/library indexing and shelving may establish accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A doctoral thesis indexed and shelved in a university library may constitute prior art if sufficiently accessible to the public interested in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General library cataloging/shelving practices (librarian affidavits) can establish accessibility (In re Hall); indexing by subject/title is important—mere filing by student name (Cronyn) or restricted access to a few persons (Bayer) may defeat public accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online database accessibility depends on findability
rubrics_metrics.description: A document in an online database is a printed publication only if an interested skilled artisan, exercising reasonable diligence, could have located it; indexing/searchability are factors but not dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexing is not necessary but is one factor (Voter Verified citing In re Lister); deficient indexing/search functionality or impractical search burden (Accel. Bay v. Activision Blizzard) can render a database item not publicly accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orally presented paper can be a printed publication when copies disseminated
rubrics_metrics.description: An oral presentation in a forum open to interested persons can be a 'printed publication' if written copies are distributed without restriction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: MIT v. AB Fortia (written copies requested/obtained), and oral presentations/demonstrations at scientific meetings or trade shows may be prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) if otherwise available to the public (see MPEP § 2152.02(e)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal confidential documents are not printed publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents distributed only internally and intended to remain confidential are not 'printed publications' regardless of number of copies—there must be an existing confidentiality policy or agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere intent to remain confidential is insufficient absent an established confidentiality arrangement; examples include in-house research reports and documents in restricted libraries (In re George; Northern Telecom v. Datapoint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public display can establish printed-publication status
rubrics_metrics.description: A publicly displayed document that persons of ordinary skill could see and were not precluded from copying can be a 'printed publication' even if not disseminated as copies or indexed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Klopfenstein factors: length of time displayed, expertise of target audience, expectations of confidentiality, and ease of copying. Temporary/transient displays may not suffice depending on these factors; cases include Klopfenstein, Medtronic v. Barry, GoPro v. Contour and Jazz Pharm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of accessibility shown by routine business practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of routine business practices (e.g., cataloging/indexing practices, distribution procedures) can establish the date on which a publication became accessible to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific evidence of typical business or library practices, affidavits, and records can substitute for direct proof of the exact date a particular document became available (Constant; In re Hall). Absent evidence of routine practices, presumptions are speculative (In re Lister).

rubrics_metrics.name: Date a mailed publication becomes prior art is date received
rubrics_metrics.description: A mailed publication (magazine, journal) becomes prior art on the date it is received by at least one member of the public, not the date mailed or sent to the publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish receipt date to determine the effective prior-art date (In re Schlittler).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions by applicant treated as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement by the applicant in the specification or during prosecution identifying another's work as 'prior art' is an admission that can be relied on for anticipation and obviousness, even if the work would not otherwise qualify as statutory prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must determine if the admitted subject matter is the inventor's own work or another's; absent a credible explanation, treat as work of another (Riverwood; Constant). Jepson-formatted preambles are taken as implied admissions unless overcome by credible explanation (In re Fout; In re Ehrreich).

rubrics_metrics.name: Listing a reference in an IDS is not an admission
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere listing of a reference in an Information Disclosure Statement (IDS) is not treated as an admission that the reference is prior art or material to patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Riverwood and 37 CFR 1.97(h): filing an IDS shall not be construed as admission that cited information is material to patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation requires every claim element in a single reference
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim as anticipated under 35 U.S.C. 102, the reference must teach each and every element of the claim, either expressly or inherently, under the claim's broadest reasonable interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The identical invention must be shown in as complete detail as in the claim; elements must be arranged as required by the claim but exact phrasing is not required (ipsissimis verbis not necessary). See Verdegaal; Richardson; MPEP § 2114.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible uses of multiple references in a 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Although normally only one reference should be used in a 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection, multiple references may be cited to (A) prove the primary reference contains an 'enabled disclosure'; (B) explain the meaning of a term used in the primary reference; or (C) show that a characteristic not disclosed is inherent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extra references and extrinsic evidence can show enablement of the primary reference (In re Samour; In re Donohue). Extrinsic evidence may explain but not expand the meaning of terms in the primary reference (In re Baxter Travenol). Use additional references only for the limited purposes above.
